decks.title: The Vedic Period — Part 1: Sources, the Family and the King, and the Assemblies
goals: Name the four Vedas and state what each contains
Explain the importance of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata as sources for the Later Vedic period
Describe the patriarchal family and the position and duties of the king in the Early Vedic period
Distinguish the Sabha, the Samiti and the Vidatha and explain how they checked the king

slides.heading: The Vedic Period: sources, king and assemblies
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we know about the Vedic age and how a tribe was governed.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the two Vedic periods and their sources, the family and the king, and the assemblies that checked the king
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: After the Harappan cities, a new way of life is described in a body of literature called the Vedas. In this part we learn what the four Vedas contain, how other works help, how the Early Vedic family and king worked, and how assemblies kept the king in check.

slides.heading: Two periods, roughly dated
slides.body_md: Historians divide the Vedic age into an **Early** and a **Later** period.

slides.narration: Historians divide the Vedic age into two periods. The Early or Rig Vedic period is dated about fifteen hundred to one thousand before the common era. The Later Vedic period runs from about one thousand to six hundred before the common era. Books differ a little on these dates, so always say about.

slides.heading: The four Vedas

rows: Hymns of praise in ten books (mandalas); the oldest
Verses arranged as melodies for chanting
Formulae and rules for performing sacrifices
Charms, spells, healing and everyday concerns

visual.alt: Table of the four Vedas: Rig Veda hymns in ten mandalas, Sama Veda melodies for chanting, Yajur Veda formulae for sacrifices, Atharva Veda charms and everyday concerns

slides.narration: There are four Vedas. The Rig Veda is the oldest and is a collection of hymns arranged in ten books called mandalas. The Sama Veda has verses set to melodies for chanting. The Yajur Veda has formulae and rules for sacrifices. The Atharva Veda has charms, spells, healing and everyday concerns.

slides.heading: Other works that help
slides.body_md: The Vedas were learnt by heart and passed on by speech long before they were written down.

rows: Society and values of the Later age

visual.alt: Table of other sources: Brahmanas explain rituals, Aranyakas are forest texts on ritual meaning, Upanishads discuss ideas, and the Ramayana and Mahabharata are epics that show society and values of the Later age

slides.narration: Other works are connected with the Vedas. The Brahmanas explain rituals. The Aranyakas, or forest texts, reflect on their meaning. The Upanishads discuss ideas and beliefs. These later works, together with the epics, help us understand the Later Vedic age. All were learnt by heart and passed on by speech for a very long time.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the Vedas
slides.body_md: Match each Veda with what it mainly contains.
slides.narration: Look back at the table of the four Vedas. Match each one with its main contents. Remember that the Rig Veda is the oldest.

slides.heading: The epics as sources
bullets: The **Ramayana**, traditionally by **Valmiki**, and the **Mahabharata**, traditionally by **Vyasa**.
They are **literary sources** for the **Later Vedic** age.
They show **family life, kingship and values**.
Read them **with care** and **together with other sources**.

nodes.label: Literary sources: family life, kingship, values

visual.alt: Flow: the Ramayana traditionally attributed to Valmiki and the Mahabharata to Vyasa are literary sources for family life, kingship and values of the Later Vedic age
visual.caption: Epics as sources (read with care).

slides.narration: The Ramayana is traditionally attributed to Valmiki and the Mahabharata to Vyasa. For students of history they are literary sources that show family life, kingship and the values people admired in the Later Vedic age. Because they are works of literature, historians read them with care and alongside other sources.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: choosing the right source
slides.body_md: Ask what you want to know, then pick the source that fits.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the question the historian is asking.
Step 2 — Decide: hymns, ritual rules, daily concerns or society?
Step 3 — Match it with the right Veda or work.
Step 4 — Add one more source if the age is the Later period.

rows: How were tribes and their gods praised in the Early age?
How was a sacrifice carried out step by step?
What daily concerns and healing practices are recorded?
What did family life and kingship look like in the Later age?

visual.alt: Table matching four historian questions with sources: hymns in the Rig Veda, sacrifice steps in the Yajur Veda and Brahmanas, daily concerns in the Atharva Veda, and Later age family life and kingship in the epics together with other sources

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. Read the question and decide whether it is about hymns, ritual rules, daily concerns or society. Then match it with the right source. Questions on the praise of gods go to the Rig Veda. Sacrifice steps go to the Yajur Veda. Healing and daily concerns go to the Atharva Veda. Society in the Later age goes to the epics with other sources.

slides.heading: Quick check: a choir leader
slides.body_md: Which Veda is closest to singing verses to tunes?
slides.narration: Think about which Veda is arranged for chanting to melodies, and which ones are about hymns, rituals or charms.

slides.heading: From family to tribe
slides.body_md: The basic unit of Early Vedic society was the **patriarchal family**.

visual.alt: Flow from the smallest to the largest unit: kula the patriarchal family, grama a village of families, vis a group of villages, jana the tribe
visual.caption: Social units, smallest to largest.

slides.narration: The basic unit of Early Vedic society was the family, called the kula. It was patriarchal, which means the father or eldest male headed it. Families together formed a village called a grama. Villages formed a larger group called a vis, and these made up the tribe, the jana.

slides.heading: The rajan: protector and leader
bullets: The **rajan** protected the tribe and led it in **war**.
He was **not an absolute ruler**.
People gave **bali**, voluntary offerings, in support.

rows: Protected the tribe; led it in war
No: assemblies and advisers checked him

visual.alt: Table on the Early Vedic family and king: the father headed the family, the rajan protected the tribe and led it in war, he was not absolute because assemblies and advisers checked him, and he was supported by voluntary offerings called bali

slides.narration: The king was called the rajan. His main duties were to protect the tribe, its people and cattle, and to lead it in war. He was not an absolute ruler, because advisers and assemblies limited him. The people supported him with voluntary offerings called bali, not with a fixed tax.

slides.heading: Officials who helped the king

rows: Priest and adviser of the rajan

visual.alt: Table of three officials: the purohita priest and adviser, the senani army commander, and the gramani village head

slides.narration: The rajan was helped by officials. The purohita was the priest and adviser who blessed the king and guided him in important matters. The senani was the commander of the army. The gramani was the head of a village. Together they carried out the daily work of the tribe.

slides.heading: Quick check: smallest to largest
slides.body_md: Arrange the Early Vedic social units from the smallest to the largest.
slides.narration: Start with the family and end with the tribe. Use the chain of units you have just seen.

slides.narration: The Early Vedic tribe had three assemblies. The Sabha was a smaller body of elders and nobles who advised the king. The Samiti was a larger assembly of the people of the tribe, linked to choosing and backing the king. The Vidatha is regarded as the oldest assembly, where tribal, religious and war matters were discussed.

slides.heading: How assemblies checked the king
bullets: The **Sabha** advised him: he did not decide alone.
The **Samiti** could **back** or **withhold** support.
The **Vidatha** gave a **tribal forum** for religious and war matters.

nodes.label: Sabha advises; Samiti backs or withholds support
Rajan needs support: power is checked

visual.alt: Flow: the rajan proposes a plan, the Sabha advises and the Samiti backs or withholds support, so the rajan needs support and his power is checked
visual.caption: How assemblies checked the king.

slides.narration: Suppose the rajan proposes a plan. The Sabha advises him on it. The Samiti may back the plan or withhold support. The Vidatha gives the tribe a place to discuss religious and war matters. Because he needs their support, the king cannot rule by his own will alone. This is how assemblies checked his power.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) Name the three assemblies. [3] (ii) Compare the Sabha and the Samiti. [3] (iii) How did assemblies check the king? [4]
bullets: (i) Three names + the Vidatha as the oldest.
(ii) One point for each, then the difference.
(iii) One point per assembly, then a closing line on limited power.
Aim for one point per mark.

rows: Three assemblies named; the Vidatha as the oldest
Sabha described; Samiti described; the difference
Role of each assembly; how the king was limited

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark answer on the assemblies: part (i) three assemblies for 3 marks, part (ii) Sabha and Samiti compared for 3 marks, part (iii) checks on the king for 4 marks

slides.narration: To plan a ten mark answer in three parts, give three points to the first part, three to the second and four to the last. Part one names the three assemblies and says the Vidatha is the oldest. Part two describes the Sabha and the Samiti and states how they differ. Part three gives a point for each assembly and ends with how the king was limited.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Say **about** with every date; books differ.
Name the **Veda** and its **contents** together.
Never write that the early king was an **absolute ruler**.
For assemblies, state **size and members** to show the difference.
Treat the epics as **literary sources**; do not claim exact dates.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Add the word about to every date. When you name a Veda, state its contents too. Never write that the Early Vedic king was an absolute ruler. For the assemblies, mention size and members to show how they differ. And treat the epics as literary sources that help us, not as exact records.

decks.title: The Vedic Period — Part 2: Economy, Women, Varnas, Ashramas and Education
goals: Compare the economy of the Early (pastoral) and Later (settled agriculture, crafts) Vedic periods
Compare the position of women in the Early and Later Vedic periods
Explain the four varnas and how they became rigid in the Later period
Describe the four ashramas and the gurukul system of education

slides.heading: Economy, women, varnas and education
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how life changed between the **Early** and **Later** Vedic ages.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the economy of the two periods, the position of women, the varnas and ashramas, and education
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we compare the economy of the two periods, see how the position of women changed, learn about the four varnas and four ashramas, and look at how students were taught in the gurukul. The aim is to describe each point factually and to compare the two periods.

slides.narration: Remember the two periods. The Early Vedic period is about fifteen hundred to one thousand before the common era, and the Later Vedic period about one thousand to six hundred before the common era. Most changes we study now happened gradually between them, not suddenly.

slides.heading: The economy compared
bullets: **Early:** mainly **pastoral**; **cattle** were wealth.
**Later:** **settled agriculture**, **iron**, crafts, trade.
Towns **began** to appear.

rows: Mostly stone, wood and copper or bronze
Iron from about 1000 BCE in some areas

visual.alt: Table comparing the Early and Later Vedic economy: main activity cattle-rearing then settled agriculture, chief wealth cattle then land, tools mostly stone wood and copper then iron from about 1000 BCE in some areas, crafts and trade limited then growing with the beginnings of towns

slides.narration: In the Early period the economy was mainly pastoral. Cattle were the chief wealth and farming was a lesser activity. In the Later period settled agriculture became important, iron appeared in some areas from about one thousand before the common era, crafts and trade grew, and the beginnings of towns appeared.

slides.heading: How iron changed farming

visual.alt: Flow: iron axes and ploughshares let farmers clear forests and plough heavy soil, giving surplus grain that supports crafts and trade and the beginnings of towns
visual.caption: How iron changed the economy.

slides.narration: Iron axes helped farmers clear forests, and iron ploughshares helped them turn heavy soil. More land under the plough meant a surplus of grain. A surplus can feed craftworkers and traders who do not farm. In this way iron helped settled agriculture, crafts, trade and the first towns to grow together.

slides.body_md: In the Early period, which was the main form of wealth?

Step 2 — Link it with herding, farming, crafts or trade.

A potter's wheel and traders' weights

slides.narration: Use four steps. Say what the object is used for. Link it with herding, farming, crafts or trade. Choose the period. Then write the reason in one line. A model herd with tiny plots belongs to the Early period. An iron ploughshare, and a potter's wheel with traders' weights, belong to the Later period.

slides.heading: Women in the two periods
bullets: **Early:** relatively **respected**; education, rituals, assemblies.
Women composers of hymns, traditionally **Ghosha, Apala, Lopamudra**.
**Later:** **excluded** from assemblies; more restrictions.

rows: Open to women; some composed hymns

slides.narration: In the Early period women were relatively respected. They could be educated, take part in rituals and assemblies, and had some choice in marriage. sections.heading: 1. The two periods and the sources
sections.body_md:
- **Early (Rig) Vedic:** about 1500 to 1000 BCE. **Later Vedic:** about 1000 to 600 BCE. Dates are approximate and vary between books; say **about**.
- **Four Vedas:** **Rig Veda** (oldest; hymns in ten mandalas, about a thousand hymns), **Sama Veda** (melodies for chanting), **Yajur Veda** (formulae and rules for sacrifices), **Atharva Veda** (charms, spells, healing, everyday concerns).
- Other works: **Brahmanas** (rituals), **Aranyakas** (forest texts), **Upanishads** (ideas).
- **Epics:** the **Ramayana** (traditionally Valmiki) and the **Mahabharata** (traditionally Vyasa) are **literary sources** for the Later Vedic age: family life, kingship, values. Read with care and with other sources.
- The texts were learnt by heart and handed down orally for a long time.

sections.heading: 2. The Early Vedic family and the king
sections.body_md:
- The **patriarchal family (kula)**, headed by the father or eldest male, was the basic unit.
- Units from smallest to largest: **kula, grama, vis, jana** (tribe).
- The **rajan** protected the tribe and led it in war; he was **not absolute**. People supported him with voluntary offerings called **bali**.
- Officials: **purohita** (priest and adviser), **senani** (army commander), **gramani** (village head).

sections.heading: 4. Economy and women: Early and Later compared
sections.body_md:
- **Early economy:** mainly **pastoral**; **cattle** were wealth; some agriculture.
- **Later economy:** **settled agriculture**; **iron** from about 1000 BCE in some areas; **crafts**, **trade** and the beginnings of **towns**.
- **Women, Early:** relatively respected: education, rituals, assemblies, some choice in marriage; women composers of hymns, traditionally Ghosha, Apala and Lopamudra.
- **Women, Later:** position declined: largely excluded from assemblies and more restrictions. Historians give different reasons for the change.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about.
- Mixing up the Sabha and the Samiti.
- Writing that the Early Vedic king was an absolute ruler.
- Treating the epics as exact records of dates.
- Confusing the four varnas with the four ashramas.
- Praising or blaming a group when describing the varnas.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A choir leader in a story set in ancient times is trained to sing verses to fixed tunes at ceremonies. Which Veda is closest to what the choir leader practises?

options.text_md: The Atharva Veda, a collection of spells
The Sama Veda, a collection arranged for chanting to melodies
The Yajur Veda, a collection of battle plans
The Rig Veda, a collection of laws

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Sama Veda, a collection arranged for chanting to melodies. The Sama Veda sets verses to melodies for singing. The Atharva Veda holds charms and everyday matters, the Yajur Veda ritual formulae, and the Rig Veda hymns, not laws or battle plans.

questions.stem_md: A label in an imagined museum corner at Vidya Niketan school reads: "Instructions the priest speaks while each step of a sacrifice is carried out." Which Veda does the label describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Yajur Veda. The Yajur Veda holds the formulae and rules spoken at each step of a sacrifice. The Sama Veda is for chanting, the Rig Veda is hymns of praise, and the Atharva Veda is about charms and daily life.

questions.stem_md: Students of Class IX-C find that one Veda has verses about healing a fever, protecting a home and winning a friend. Which Veda is it most likely to be?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Atharva Veda. Spells, charms, healing and everyday concerns are typical of the Atharva Veda. The Sama Veda is melodies, the Yajur Veda ritual formulae, and the Rig Veda mostly hymns to the gods.

questions.stem_md: A teacher at an imagined school in Kaveripur asks which additional literary works help a student studying Later Vedic society after the Rig Veda. Which answer is most suitable?

options.text_md: The accounts of travellers from a much later age only
Newspaper reports from the last century
The Ramayana and the Mahabharata, whose stories reflect the society and values of that age
Only the Sama Veda, since it is the largest Veda

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Ramayana and the Mahabharata, whose stories reflect the society and values of that age. The two epics, treated as literary sources, give a picture of family life, kingship and values of the Later Vedic age. Later travellers and modern papers are too far removed, and the Sama Veda is about chanting.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined history club says, "The Rig Veda alone can tell us everything about life in every Vedic age." Which reply is the most accurate?

options.text_md: It is correct, because the Rig Veda is the only Vedic source
It is wrong, because the Rig Veda says nothing about society
It mainly reflects the Early Vedic period, so other texts and the epics help to learn about Later Vedic life
It is correct, because every Veda was composed in a single year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It mainly reflects the Early Vedic period, so other texts and the epics help to learn about Later Vedic life. The Rig Veda is the chief source for the Early period; for the Later period historians also use the other Vedas, the Brahmanas, the Upanishads and the epics. It does describe society, and the Vedas were not composed in a single year.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Ramayana and the Mahabharata are used as literary sources for Later Vedic society.

**Reason (R):** The epics give the exact date and the exact place of every event they describe.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: the epics help to picture social life and ideas. R is false: they are works of literature and do not supply exact dates or places for every event.

questions.stem_md: The four Vedas are the Rig Veda, the Sama Veda, the ___ Veda and the Atharva Veda.
questions.solution_md: The third Veda is the Yajur Veda.

questions.stem_md: Match each Veda with what it mainly contains.

match_right.text_md: Verses set to melodies for chanting
Hymns of praise in ten books

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The Rig Veda is hymns, the Sama Veda melodies, the Yajur Veda ritual formulae and the Atharva Veda charms and daily life.

questions.stem_md: Why are the Ramayana and the Mahabharata useful to a student of Later Vedic society?
questions.solution_md: Literary sources; picture of society.

answer.model_answer_md: The two epics are **literary sources** whose stories show **family life, kingship and social values** of the later age. They help us picture society, though they are not exact records of dates.

marking_scheme.step: Literary sources of the Later Vedic age
Show social life and values; not exact records

questions.stem_md: A museum label in an imagined gallery says, "Verses meant to be sung to tunes at a ceremony." Name the Veda described and name one other Veda with its contents.
questions.solution_md: Sama Veda and one other Veda.

answer.model_answer_md: The label describes the **Sama Veda**, verses set to melodies for chanting. Another is the **Yajur Veda**, which has **formulae and rules** for performing sacrifices.

questions.stem_md: A group in the imagined Class IX-A uses a story from the Mahabharata to describe Later Vedic society. State two things such a source can tell us and one caution a historian must keep in mind.
questions.solution_md: Two uses and one caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It shows **how people lived**, such as family ties and the duties of rulers.
2. It reveals **values and beliefs** admired in that age.
3. **Caution:** the epic is a work of **literature**, composed and retold over time, so it must be read with other sources and not as an exact record of dates.

marking_scheme.step: Caution: literature, read with other sources

questions.stem_md: Which description best fits the rajan of the Early Vedic tribe?

options.text_md: A leader who protected the tribe and led it in war, but did not rule without checks
An absolute ruler who made every decision alone
A priest who took no part in war
A trader who ran markets in towns

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A leader who protected the tribe and led it in war, but did not rule without checks. The rajan protected the tribe and led in battle, while assemblies and customs limited him. He was not absolute, he was not mainly a priest, and towns and markets belong more to the Later period.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined role-play of a tribe called the Devapura jana, the rajan must pick someone to command the fighting men before a cattle raid. Which officer takes this role?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The senani. The senani led the army. The purohita was the priest and adviser, the gramani headed a village, and the vidatha was an assembly, not an officer.

questions.stem_md: In the same imagined role-play, one character blesses the rajan before a journey and advises him in important matters. Which official does this character represent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The purohita. The purohita was the chief priest and adviser of the rajan. The senani commanded the army, the gramani led a village, and the vis was a division of the tribe, not an official.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is the strongest reason why the Early Vedic king cannot be called an absolute ruler?

options.text_md: Assemblies of the tribe and the advice of officials limited his decisions
He did not own any cattle
He was chosen by a foreign power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Assemblies of the tribe and the advice of officials limited his decisions. The Sabha, the Samiti and the Vidatha, together with the counsel of officers such as the purohita, checked the rajan. The other options are not true of the tribal king.

questions.stem_md: In Early Vedic society the people gave the rajan offerings called bali. What does this show about the king?

options.text_md: He had no duties towards the people
He was supported by gifts from the tribe in return for protecting it, rather than by a fixed regular tax
He collected a fixed tax from every house every month
He ruled a large empire with a paid army

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** He was supported by gifts from the tribe in return for protecting it, rather than by a fixed regular tax. Bali was an offering made by the people, which fits the picture of a protector supported by his tribe. A fixed monthly tax or a vast empire belongs to a later and more developed state.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The rajan of the Early Vedic tribe was expected to protect his people.

**Reason (R):** He led the tribe in war and defended its cattle and land.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Leading in war and defending the tribe are exactly the ways in which the rajan protected his people.

questions.stem_md: In the Early Vedic period the largest social unit, the tribe, was called the ___.
questions.solution_md: The tribe was the jana.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these Early Vedic social units from the smallest to the largest.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Family, village, group of villages, tribe.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two duties of the king in the Early Vedic period.
questions.solution_md: Two duties.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He **protected the tribe**, its people, cattle and land.
2. He **led the tribe in war** against raiders and rival tribes.

questions.stem_md: Name any two officials who helped the Early Vedic king and state what each did.
questions.solution_md: Two officials with their roles.

answer.model_answer_md: The **purohita** was the priest and adviser of the king. The **senani** commanded the army. (The **gramani** headed a village.)

questions.stem_md: In an imagined role-play, a rajan says he alone will decide whether the tribe moves its herds to a new valley. Explain why a student playing a historian could say this does not match the Early Vedic idea of kingship.
questions.solution_md: Protector, not absolute; assemblies and advisers.

answer.model_answer_md: In the Early period the rajan was a **protector and war leader**, not an absolute ruler. **Assemblies** of the tribe and the advice of **officials** shared in important decisions, so he could not decide alone.

marking_scheme.step: Rajan as protector and war leader, not absolute

questions.stem_md: Describe the Early Vedic family and the position of the king in three points.
questions.solution_md: Family, units, king.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **family (kula)** was the basic unit and was **patriarchal**, headed by the father.
2. Families formed a **grama**, villages a **vis**, and these made up the **jana**, or tribe.
3. The **rajan** protected the tribe and led it in war, but **assemblies** and officials limited his power.

marking_scheme.step: Chain of units up to the jana
Position of the king, with limits

questions.stem_md: Which assembly is considered the oldest, dealing with tribal, religious and military matters?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Vidatha. The Vidatha is regarded as the oldest assembly, with tribal, religious and military functions. The Sabha and the Samiti are other assemblies, and a Brahmana is a text or a varna, not an assembly.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined role-play at Class IX-B, a rajan wishes to start a long war, but all the senior elders and nobles gathered in a small meeting advise against it. Which assembly do they represent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Sabha. A small body of elders and nobles giving advice is the Sabha. The Samiti is the larger assembly of the people; a gurukul is a school and a kula is a family.

questions.stem_md: In another imagined role-play, hundreds of members of the Devapura jana gather in an open field to hear and voice opinions on who should be their next rajan. Which assembly is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Samiti. A large gathering of the tribe, linked to choosing and backing the king, is the Samiti. The Sabha is small, the aranyaka is a text, and the senani is an army commander.

questions.stem_md: How did the assemblies act as a check on the power of the Early Vedic king?

options.text_md: They removed the army from his control permanently
They gave the king the right to collect any tax he liked
They discussed matters and advised or backed him, so he needed their support to rule
They decided the date of every festival only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They discussed matters and advised or backed him, so he needed their support to rule. Assemblies advised the king and gave or withheld support, which restrained one-man rule. They did not take away the army forever, licence unlimited taxes, or deal only with festivals.

questions.stem_md: A student notes in an imagined project: "Sabha: whole tribe; Samiti: elders only; Vidatha: oldest assembly." Which correction is right?

options.text_md: The Sabha and the Samiti were the same body
The Sabha was the smaller body of elders and the Samiti the larger assembly of the people
The Vidatha was the newest assembly
The Samiti never met the king

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Sabha was the smaller body of elders and the Samiti the larger assembly of the people. The student has swapped the Sabha and the Samiti. The Vidatha is called the oldest, so it was not the newest, and the Samiti and the Sabha were distinct bodies that both dealt with the king.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Vidatha is regarded as the oldest of the Early Vedic assemblies.

**Reason (R):** The Sabha was a smaller body of elders.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but the size of the Sabha does not explain why the Vidatha is called the oldest assembly.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If an imagined rajan found that both the Sabha and the Samiti opposed a plan, he would have found it hard to carry the plan through.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Because the assemblies could advise and give or withhold support, their joint opposition would limit the king.

questions.stem_md: The two best known Early Vedic assemblies are the Sabha and the ___, and the oldest one is the Vidatha.
questions.solution_md: The other well-known assembly was the Samiti.

questions.stem_md: Match each assembly with its description.

match_right.text_md: Oldest assembly with tribal, religious and military matters
Smaller body of elders and nobles

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(q), (c)–(p). Sabha, small body of elders; Samiti, large assembly; Vidatha, the oldest assembly.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the Sabha and the Samiti.
questions.solution_md: Small body of elders versus large assembly.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Sabha** was a **small body of elders and nobles** that gave the king advice. The **Samiti** was a **large gathering of the people of the tribe**.

marking_scheme.step: Samiti: larger assembly of the people

questions.stem_md: In an imagined tribe the rajan proposes to move the herds to a new valley, and the elders object. How does this show an assembly acting as a check?
questions.solution_md: Elders object; king needs support.

answer.model_answer_md: The **elders** of the **Sabha** advise against the plan, and the king needs their **support** to proceed. The assembly thus **limits** the king and prevents him from acting **alone**.

questions.stem_md: In three points, explain how the assemblies checked the power of the king in the Early Vedic period.
questions.solution_md: Three assemblies, three checks.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Sabha** of elders **advised** the king, so he did not decide alone.
2. The **Samiti** of the people could **back or withhold support**, which mattered for his position.
3. The **Vidatha** gave a **tribal forum** for religious and war matters, so these were not settled by one man.

questions.stem_md: In the Early Vedic period, which of the following was the most important form of wealth?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cattle. The economy was mainly pastoral, so cattle were wealth. Iron tools and towns grew in the Later period, and a coin treasury does not describe the Early age.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the position of women in the Early Vedic period?

options.text_md: Women were barred from all education and religion
Women were relatively respected and could be educated and take part in rituals and assemblies
Women could not take part in any family decision

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Women were relatively respected and could be educated and take part in rituals and assemblies. The Early period shows women as relatively well regarded: education, participation in rituals and assemblies, and some choice in marriage. They did not rule every tribe, nor were they shut out of everything.

questions.stem_md: Which of these names is traditionally associated with a woman who composed hymns in the Early Vedic age?

options.text_md: Valmiki, traditional author of the Ramayana
Vyasa, traditional author of the Mahabharata
The senani of an imagined tribe

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lopamudra. Lopamudra, along with Ghosha and Apala, is traditionally named as a woman composer of hymns. Valmiki and Vyasa are traditional authors of the epics, and a senani is an army commander.

questions.stem_md: A historian in an imagined seminar notes that women in the Later Vedic age were seldom seen in assemblies and faced more restrictions. What does this show about the Later period?

options.text_md: A decline in the position of women compared with the Early period
An improvement in the position of women
No change at all in the position of women
That women began to lead every assembly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A decline in the position of women compared with the Early period. Exclusion from assemblies and growing restrictions point to a lower status than in the Early period. It was not an improvement or a constant, and women did not lead every assembly.

questions.stem_md: Why did the use of iron, from about 1000 BCE in some areas, matter for Later Vedic society?

options.text_md: Iron replaced all cattle in the economy at once
Iron tools helped to clear forests and plough heavy soil, so settled agriculture grew
Iron was used only to make coins

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Iron tools helped to clear forests and plough heavy soil, so settled agriculture grew. Iron axes and ploughs made it easier to clear land and farm it, supporting settled agriculture. Cattle remained valuable, trade grew rather than ended, and iron was not used only for coins.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum case shows an iron ploughshare, a potter's wheel and traders' weights. To which period does the case most likely belong?

options.text_md: The period of the Harappan cities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Later Vedic period. Iron tools, crafts and trade suggest the Later Vedic economy of settled farming and growing crafts. The Early period was mainly pastoral, and the other periods are earlier.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined museum labels read: Label 1, "Herds were counted as riches; fields were small." Label 2, "Villages depended on ploughed fields and crafts; towns were beginning." Which pairing is correct?

options.text_md: Label 1 is Early Vedic and Label 2 is Later Vedic
Label 1 is Later Vedic and Label 2 is Early Vedic

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Label 1 is Early Vedic and Label 2 is Later Vedic. Herds as wealth with small fields belong to the pastoral Early period, while ploughed fields, crafts and early towns belong to the Later period. The other pairings reverse or ignore this contrast.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best explains the link between the changing economy and the lower position of women in the Later Vedic age, as some historians suggest?

options.text_md: The invention of coins made all women wealthy
The assemblies were closed to men
The tribes stopped living in families
As settled farming grew, property and family roles became more fixed, and women's public role narrowed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** As settled farming grew, property and family roles became more fixed, and women's public role narrowed. Some historians link settled agriculture and property with more rigid roles and fewer public opportunities for women. The other options do not match the evidence, and this is an interpretation, not a settled fact.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Settled agriculture grew in the Later Vedic period.

**Reason (R):** The use of iron tools made it easier to clear land and plough the soil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Iron tools helped farmers clear and plough land, which is a main reason settled agriculture spread.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The economy of the Early Vedic period was mainly pastoral, with agriculture as a lesser activity.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Cattle-rearing was the mainstay of the Early period, and farming was less important.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature with what it points to in Vedic history.

match_right.text_md: Decline in the position of women
Settled agriculture of the Later period
Pastoral economy of the Early period

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Cattle point to the pastoral Early economy, iron to Later settled agriculture, the three names to women hymn-composers, and exclusion from assemblies to the later decline in the position of women.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which women were relatively respected in the Early Vedic period.
questions.solution_md: Any two.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Women could receive **education**; some composed **hymns**, such as **Ghosha, Apala and Lopamudra**.
2. They could take part in **rituals and assemblies** and had some **choice in marriage**.

questions.stem_md: How did the position of women change in the Later Vedic period?
questions.solution_md: Decline, with a sign.

answer.model_answer_md: It **declined**. Women were largely **excluded from assemblies** and faced more **restrictions** on education and freedom than in the Early period.

marking_scheme.step: Declined relative to the Early period
One sign: exclusion from assemblies or restrictions

questions.stem_md: An imagined village in the Later Vedic age receives iron axes and ploughshares. State two effects this could have on its economy.
questions.solution_md: Two effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Forests could be cleared** and heavy soil ploughed, so **settled agriculture** expanded.
2. A surplus of grain could support **crafts and trade**, helping the beginnings of **towns**.

marking_scheme.step: Surplus supporting crafts, trade and towns

questions.stem_md: Compare the position of women in the Early and Later Vedic periods in three points.
questions.solution_md: Education; assemblies; overall change.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Early:** women were relatively respected and could receive **education**; some, like **Ghosha**, composed hymns.
2. **Early:** they took part in **rituals and assemblies**; **Later:** they were largely **excluded** from assemblies.
3. **Later:** the position **declined**, with more **restrictions** on their freedom.

questions.stem_md: Compare the Early and the Later Vedic economy on wealth, farming and crafts.
questions.solution_md: Three contrasts.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Wealth:** in the Early period **cattle** were the chief wealth; in the Later period **land and produce** mattered more.
2. **Farming:** **pastoral** economy with some farming, then **settled agriculture** with iron tools.
3. **Crafts:** limited at first, then **crafts, trade and the beginnings of towns** grew.

questions.stem_md: Some historians link the changes in the Later Vedic economy to changes in society. Give three such links, and say why they are interpretations.
questions.solution_md: Three links and the caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Settled **agriculture** and **iron** supported more **permanent villages** and early towns.
2. Growing **property** and **crafts** made roles in society more **fixed**.
3. Some link this to the **narrowing of women's public role**. These are **interpretations**: the sources are literary and historians **weigh them differently**.

marking_scheme.step: Women's role; the caution of interpretation

questions.stem_md: Which list gives the four varnas of Vedic society?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. The four varnas were the Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. The second list gives the ashramas, the third the Vedas, and the fourth the social units.

questions.stem_md: How is the varna system described in the Early Vedic period?

options.text_md: It was fairly flexible and linked mainly to occupation
It was fixed by birth from the start
It did not exist in any form
It was limited to one tribe

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It was fairly flexible and linked mainly to occupation. In the Early period divisions were fairly flexible and tied to work, and only later hardened. They were not fixed by birth from the start, and they were not absent or limited to one tribe.

questions.stem_md: An imagined historian explains that, in the Later Vedic period, a child belonged to the varna of the family into which the child was born, whatever work the child chose. What change in the varna system is being described?

options.text_md: The system became rigid and birth-based
The system became based on wealth alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The system became rigid and birth-based. Membership by birth irrespective of occupation is what historians mean by a rigid, birth-based system. It had not become more flexible, ended or turned into a wealth-based division.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined role-play, a character runs a home, raises a family and earns a living. Which ashrama does the character represent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Grihastha. The householder stage is Grihastha. Brahmacharya is student life, Vanaprastha a gradual withdrawal from worldly duties, and Sannyasa a life of renunciation.

questions.stem_md: How did students mainly learn in the gurukul of the Vedic age?

options.text_md: Through examinations set by the king
Orally: by listening, reciting and memorising under the teacher

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Orally: by listening, reciting and memorising under the teacher. Learning was oral: students listened, recited and memorised. Printed books, paper and royal examinations did not exist in this form.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the later varna hierarchy is the most balanced for a history exam?

options.text_md: It gave equal rights to every group and was therefore fair to all
It should be praised as a perfect system
It should be ignored because it had no effect on society
As a rigid, birth-based hierarchy it created inequality, and historians study it to understand how society changed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** As a rigid, birth-based hierarchy it created inequality, and historians study it to understand how society changed. A neutral account says the system hardened into a birth-based order that produced inequality, and historians examine this to understand social change. Praising or ignoring it, or calling it equal, does not fit the evidence.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined class says that a person who has left home to live a simple life in the forest, handing worldly duties to the next generation, is in the stage just after Grihastha. Which stage is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Vanaprastha. Vanaprastha follows Grihastha, with a gradual withdrawal from worldly duties. Brahmacharya comes first, Sannyasa is the final stage of renunciation, and a gurukul is a school, not an ashrama.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the Later Vedic period the varna divisions became rigid and birth-based.

**Reason (R):** In the Later period a person could freely change varna by changing occupation.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md:
The history of the Vedic period is learnt mainly from literature.

(i) Name the four Vedas. **[3]**
(ii) State what the Rig Veda and any one other Veda contain. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the importance of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata as sources for the Later Vedic period, with one caution. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Four Vedas; contents of two; importance of the epics with a caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The four Vedas are the **Rig Veda**, the **Sama Veda**, the **Yajur Veda** and the **Atharva Veda**; the **Rig Veda** is the oldest.

(ii) The **Rig Veda** is a collection of **hymns** in ten books called mandalas. The **Sama Veda** has verses arranged as **melodies** for chanting (the Yajur Veda has ritual formulae, the Atharva Veda charms and everyday matters).

(iii) The epics are **literary sources** that show **family life, kingship and values** of the Later Vedic age, so they help to picture society beyond the Vedas. A historian must be cautious: they are works of **literature**, composed and retold over time, so they are read **together with other sources** and not taken as exact records of dates.

questions.stem_md:
Early Vedic society was organised around the family and the tribe.

(i) Describe the Early Vedic family and arrange the social units from the smallest to the largest. **[3]**
(ii) State the duties of the rajan. **[3]**
(iii) Why was the king not an absolute ruler? Name two officials who helped him. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Family and units; duties; limits and officials.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **family (kula)** was **patriarchal**, headed by the father. Families formed a **grama** (village), villages a **vis**, and these made up the **jana**, the tribe.

(ii) The **rajan** was the **protector of the tribe**, defending its people, cattle and land, and the **leader in war**. He also took part in the ceremonies of the tribe.

(iii) He was not absolute because **assemblies** such as the Sabha and the Samiti advised him and could withhold support, and because **customs** guided him. The **purohita**, the priest and adviser, and the **senani**, the commander of the army, helped him; the **gramani** headed a village.

questions.stem_md:
The Early Vedic tribe had assemblies as well as a king.

(i) Name the three assemblies and say which one is regarded as the oldest. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the Sabha and the Samiti, showing how they differed. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the assemblies checked the power of the king. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three assemblies; two compared; checks on the king.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The three assemblies were the **Sabha**, the **Samiti** and the **Vidatha**; the **Vidatha** is regarded as the **oldest**.

(ii) The **Sabha** was a **small body of elders and nobles** that gave the king advice. The **Samiti** was a **wider assembly of the people of the tribe**, associated with choosing and backing the king. They differed in size and membership.

(iii) The king needed the **support** of the assemblies. The Sabha **advised** him, so he did not decide alone; the Samiti could **back or withhold** support; and the Vidatha gave the tribe a **forum** for religious and war matters. Together they **limited one-man rule** and made the king **answerable** to the tribe.

questions.stem_md:
Society and economy changed from the Early to the Later Vedic period.

(i) Compare the economy of the two periods in three points. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the position of women in the Early period. **[3]**
(iii) How did the position of women change in the Later period, and why do historians offer different reasons for this change? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Economy compared; women in the Early period; change and interpretations.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Early:** mainly **pastoral**, with **cattle** as wealth and little farming. **Later:** **settled agriculture** with **iron tools** became important, and **crafts, trade** and the beginnings of **towns** grew.

(ii) Women were **relatively respected**: they could receive **education**, some composed **hymns** (Ghosha, Apala, Lopamudra), took part in **rituals and assemblies**, and had some **choice in marriage**.

(iii) In the Later period their position **declined**: they were largely **excluded from assemblies** and faced more **restrictions**. Historians offer **different reasons**: some point to **settled agriculture and property**, others to changes in ritual and law. The sources are **literary**, so the evidence is read in more than one way.

questions.stem_md:
Vedic society was shaped by the varnas and the ashramas.

(i) Name the four varnas and explain how the system changed from the Early to the Later period. **[3]**
(ii) Name the four ashramas in order and describe any two. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the gurukul system of education: its place, method and subjects. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Varnas and change; ashramas; gurukul.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The varnas were the **Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras**. In the **Early** period the divisions were **flexible** and linked to **occupation**; in the **Later** period they became **rigid and birth-based**, a hierarchy that later caused inequality.

(ii) The ashramas were **Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa**. In **Brahmacharya** the person was a **student**; in **Grihastha** a **householder**, earning a living and raising a family.

(iii) **Place:** the **gurukul**, where students lived with the teacher. **Method:** **oral**, by listening, reciting and memorising. **Subjects:** the **Vedas** and rituals, language and grammar, and skills linked to a student's work, such as warfare for future warriors.

questions.stem_md:
Two imagined museum rooms show the Vedic world. Room A displays herds, a rajan with a purohita and a senani, and women chanting hymns at an assembly. Room B displays iron ploughshares, a pottery workshop, a market scene and a household in which women stay indoors.

(i) Identify the period of each room with one reason each. **[3]**
(ii) Explain what Room A tells us about the king and the family. **[3]**
(iii) Explain what the change from Room A to Room B shows about the economy and the position of women. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Periods with reasons; Room A on king and family; change in economy and women.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Room A is **Early Vedic**: herds point to a **pastoral** economy and women at assemblies to their respect. Room B is **Later Vedic**: **iron ploughshares**, crafts and markets show settled agriculture and trade.

(ii) The rajan is a **protector and leader in war**, advised by the **purohita** and the **senani**, so he is not absolute. The family is **patriarchal** but women take part in **ritual and assembly**.

(iii) The economy moved from **cattle-rearing** to **settled agriculture, crafts and trade**. The position of women **declined**, as they were **excluded from assemblies** and faced restrictions; some historians link the two changes, while others stress other causes.

questions.stem_md:
A student in an imagined debate says: "Because we know of the Vedic age only from texts, we cannot say anything reliable about its society."

(i) Name the kinds of texts that give us information about the Vedic age. **[3]**
(ii) Give two features of Early Vedic government that these texts describe. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the student's view: how far is it fair, and how should a historian use such texts? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Kinds of texts; two features; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **four Vedas** (above all the **Rig Veda**), the **Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads**, and the **epics**, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, for the Later age.

(ii) The **rajan** as protector and war leader, helped by officials such as the **purohita** and the **senani**; and **assemblies**, the Sabha, the Samiti and the Vidatha, which checked him.

(iii) The view is **partly fair**: the texts are literary, mostly religious, and composed and retold over time, so they give a **partial** picture and are hard to date exactly. But they are **not useless**: read **together**, compared with each other and with other evidence, they show **consistent features** of society. A historian therefore uses them **carefully**, notes their **limits** and says **about** when giving dates.
